```{r setup}
library(yourhonor)
```

`agreement()` reports two lower bounds for every coefficient: `conf_low`, the
lower end of the percentile item bootstrap, and `conf_low_exact`, a bound that
uses no resampling at all. An acceptance policy assesses the smaller of the
two (`?acceptance_policy`). This article says what `conf_low_exact` bounds,
how it is built, and where it is strong or weak. The help page `?agreement`
keeps only what the column is.

## Why a second bound

The percentile bootstrap is optimistic exactly where an audit is most
tempted to trust it. On a perfect sample every resample is perfect too, so the
interval has zero width at 1:

```{r}
perfect <- data.frame(human = rep(c("I", "P", "C"), 10))
perfect$judge <- perfect$human
exact_demo <- agreement(perfect, n_boot = 200, seed = 1, label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"))
exact_demo[, c("coefficient", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high", "conf_low_exact", "ci_reliable")]
```

That interval is flagged `ci_reliable = FALSE` rather than read as proof of
population-perfect agreement, and `conf_low_exact` is the usable lower bound
there. The bootstrap is also optimistic at small `n` (around 30 items or
fewer), which is why policies read both.

## What it bounds

Each coefficient is `(pa - pe) / (1 - pe)`, where `pa` is its observed
agreement and `pe` its chance term. `conf_low_exact` is a lower bound on the
coefficient's own `pa`, mapped onto its scale as `(lower - pe) / (1 - pe)`
with the sample's chance term `pe` held fixed, then capped as described under
[The cap](#the-cap).

`pa` is the mean over items of each item's weighted pairwise agreement, so a
near miss under weights earns its partial credit. Krippendorff's alpha's `pa`
is `(1 - eps) * A + eps`, with `A` the mean weighted by each item's number of
ratings `r` and `eps = 1 / sum(r)`, and its bound is on `A`.

Each item's agreement is bounded by the declared weights' range, 0 to 1, not
by the weights between the categories the sample happened to show: a rare,
distant disagreement the sample missed would otherwise make the bound
overshoot. Declaring a level beyond the observed ones therefore lowers
kappa's and alpha's bound even where it leaves their estimates unchanged
(the weighted estimates' dependence on unused levels is described in
`?agreement`).

## Which inequality

The bound is one-sided at level `(1 + conf_level) / 2`, like the lower end of
the bootstrap interval.

- With two raters and no weights each item agrees or not, and the bound is
  Clopper-Pearson's.
- Otherwise each item's agreement lies between 0 and 1, and the bound is the
  binomial stop-loss bound for a mean of such values, which is never looser
  than Hoeffding's.
- For alpha with three or more rater columns it bounds alpha's ratio of
  rating-weighted agreement by inverting Hoeffding's relative-entropy test,
  so missing ratings widen it.

On a perfect sample every route gives Clopper-Pearson's
`((1 - conf_level) / 2)^(1 / n)` on `pa` for `n` items, except alpha with
missing ratings, which is lower. In the sample above, `n = 30` and every
coefficient's chance term is `1/3`, so the bound on `pa` and its image on the
coefficient's scale are:

```{r}
lower_pa <- ((1 - 0.95) / 2)^(1 / 30)
lower_pa
(lower_pa - 1 / 3) / (1 - 1 / 3)
```

which is the `conf_low_exact` of `r round(exact_demo$conf_low_exact[1], 3)`
reported above.

## The cap

No sample's bound ranks above that of a perfect sample it can be corrected
into. A correction gives every item whose ratings disagree one of its own
ratings for all of them (in a calibration, the judge matching the human
reference) and keeps the other items and the missing ratings. The bound is
capped at the worst such perfect sample's (for Gwet's coefficients, at or
below it: their chance term is bounded from above rather than found exactly).

Without the cap an error could rank above its own correction, because a
rating moved into a rarer category, or into one the perfect sample never
used, raises the chance disagreement `1 - pe` that divides the bound's
margin. The cap costs most at small `n` with rare categories, where a rare
category seen only in disagreements lets a correction drop it: in simulation
with 20 to 30 items and end categories of 1% to 3%, the share of samples
whose AC2 bound reached 0.6 fell from 12% to 1% in the worst scenario (three
raters, end categories of 3%, 30 items), while coverage was unchanged; from
100 items it moved the mean bound by about 0.004 at most.

Two imperfect samples keep no such guarantee: correcting an error can lower
the estimate itself (when it removes the only rating in a category from the
chance term), so no bound that tracks the estimate can always rise with a
correction.

## How fast it tightens

As items accumulate the bound approaches the estimate, at a rate of about
`1 / sqrt(n)`, for every coefficient, weighting and number of raters,
provided `1 - pe` stays away from 0, for the corrections too. For kappa and
alpha that holds when the items the raters agree on use at least two
categories in non-vanishing shares. Gwet's chance term for a correction
always stays below 1, but on a wide quadratic scale the gap can be small
(about 0.02 with six levels), so the cap can hold the bound down until a few
thousand items.

## Exact for what

It is exact (a finite-sample bound, not an asymptotic one) for observed
agreement, not for the coefficient, because `pe` is itself estimated. In
simulation (two and several raters, weighted and not, alpha with missing
ratings, 30 to 1000 items) its coverage of the coefficient was at or above
nominal, within simulation error. It does not depend on resampling, so it
stays honest where the percentile bootstrap is optimistic: at small `n`, and
on a perfect sample.

## Where it is weak

Because the bound on observed agreement is divided by `1 - pe`, it is weak
for kappa and alpha on imbalanced labels, whose `pe` is large. At 90/10
prevalence it stays far below the estimate until a few hundred items (a kappa
of 0.92 on 100 items averaged about 0.63 in simulation), and it can fall
below -1 (kappa's floor is `-pe / (1 - pe)`). Gwet's AC1 has a small `pe`
there and is affected far less. One sample of 100 items at 90/10, with one
error in each direction:

```{r}
human <- c(rep("pass", 90), rep("fail", 10))
judge <- human
judge[c(1, 95)] <- c("fail", "pass")
imbalanced <- agreement(data.frame(human = human, judge = judge), n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
imbalanced[, c("coefficient", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_low_exact")]
```

## What a policy reads

`conf_low_exact` never exceeds `estimate`, is reported for every coefficient
with `status = "ok"`, and is `NA` otherwise. A policy's
`min_agreement_lower` is checked against the smaller of `conf_low` and
`conf_low_exact`, so a judge passes only when both the bootstrap and the
exact bound clear the floor.
